result.markdown: --- title: "Nonuniform grids" subtitle: "ConvolutionInterpolations.jl against Interpolations.jl, BSplineKit.jl and Dierckx.jl on nonuniform knots" engine: julia --- Interpolation from samples whose spacing varies: the nonuniform convolution kernels against the methods of the other packages that accept arbitrary knots — the gridded linear interpolant of Interpolations.jl, the B-spline interpolants of BSplineKit.jl at cubic and high order, and the quintic FITPACK spline of Dierckx.jl — and against the package's own other route, which treats the samples as scattered points and fits a uniform-grid interpolant through them exactly (`fit_scattered` with `mode = :exact`). First the convergence order on jittered knots, which is the claim to verify: on nonuniform grids the `b` kernels converge at order degree + 1, so `:b13` is a 14th-order interpolant. Then the time to construct and to evaluate, and the two together. ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Packages, the methods and the knots"} using ConvolutionInterpolations import Interpolations # qualified: exports `interpolate`, as BSplineKit does import BSplineKit import Dierckx using Chairmarks, Printf, Random, CairoMakie # each method maps a vector of knots x (uniform or not) and the values y to a callable # interpolant, in the element type of x — Float64 or BigFloat. Dierckx is Float64 only, so it # is given Float64 copies and evaluated in Float64 whatever it is asked for methods_1d = [ "Interpolations.jl linear" => (x, y) -> Interpolations.interpolate((x,), y, Interpolations.Gridded(Interpolations.Linear())), "BSplineKit k=4" => (x, y) -> BSplineKit.interpolate(x, y, BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(4)), "BSplineKit k=8" => (x, y) -> BSplineKit.interpolate(x, y, BSplineKit.BSplineOrder(8)), "Dierckx k=5" => (x, y) -> (s = Dierckx.Spline1D(Float64.(x), Float64.(y); k = 5); t -> s(Float64(t))), "ConvInterp :n3" => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :n3), "ConvInterp :b5" => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b5), "ConvInterp :b7" => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7), "ConvInterp :b13" => (x, y) -> convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b13), # the samples as scattered points, fitted exactly by a uniform-grid interpolant (default :b5) "fit_scattered :exact" => (x, y) -> (f = convolution_interpolation(reshape(Float64.(x), 1, :), Float64.(y); mode = :exact); t -> f(Float64(t))), ] runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2) # Runge's function, in the type of x # n knots on [-1, 1] in the element type T: uniform, or jittered — uniform knots moved by up to # ±15 % of the spacing, with the end knots fixed, which is nonuniform without any structure a # method could exploit. The jitter is drawn once in Float64 from a seeded generator and # widened, so the knots are the same numbers in every precision uniform(T, n) = collect(range(T(-1), T(1), length = n)) function jittered(T, n) x = uniform(T, n) h = 2 / T(n - 1) x[2:end-1] .+= 0.3h .* (T.(rand(MersenneTwister(1), n - 2)) .- 0.5) x end # the largest error of every method on the fine points xr, for knots x function errors(x, xr) y = runge.(x) Dict(name => maximum(abs.(m(x, y).(xr) .- runge.(xr))) for (name, m) in methods_1d) end xr = range(-1.0, 1.0, length = 2001); # the fine points, in Float64 ``` ::: ## The knots Forty-one knots, uniform and jittered, under the function they sample: ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The two grids"} fig = Figure(size = (800, 320)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x", ylabel = "f(x)") lines!(ax, xr, runge.(xr); color = :black, label = "Runge's function") scatter!(ax, uniform(Float64, 41), fill(-0.08, 41); marker = :vline, markersize = 14, label = "uniform knots") scatter!(ax, jittered(Float64, 41), fill(-0.18, 41); marker = :vline, markersize = 14, label = "jittered knots") Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Convergence order The largest error against Runge's function as the number of jittered knots doubles, in `Float64` on the left and in `BigFloat` at 128 bits on the right, with reference lines of slope 6 through `:b5` and slope 14 through `:b13`. On a uniform grid the `b` kernels are designed for 7th-order convergence, whatever their degree. On a nonuniform grid their weights are built per interval, by projecting the kernel onto polynomial reproduction up to the kernel's full degree, and the convergence order becomes degree + 1: 6 for `:b5`, 8 for `:b7`, 14 for `:b13`. In `Float64` every method stops at rounding, and the question is which gets there first; the Julia package is generic over the element type, so the same study in `BigFloat` shows the orders over the whole range. Dierckx is `Float64` only and stays at its floor on the right. ::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The convergence study"} ns = [21, 41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281, 2561, 5121] errs_f = [errors(jittered(Float64, n), xr) for n in ns] errs_b = setprecision(BigFloat, 128) do xr_b = range(big(-1), big(1), length = 2001) [errors(jittered(BigFloat, n), xr_b) for n in ns] end # reference lines anchored at 41 knots, where the kernels are past their coarsest-grid behaviour ref(e41, p) = e41 .* (40 ./ (ns .- 1)) .^ p fig = Figure(size = (800, 520)) ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "knots", ylabel = "largest error", title = "Float64") ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "knots", title = "BigFloat, 128 bits") for (ax, errs, floor) in ((ax1, errs_f, 1e-17), (ax2, errs_b, 1e-36)) for (name, _) in methods_1d scatterlines!(ax, ns, [max(Float64(e[name]), floor) for e in errs]; markersize = 8, label = name) end lines!(ax, ns, max.(ref(Float64(errs[2]["ConvInterp :b5"]), 6), floor); color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "slope 6") lines!(ax, ns, max.(ref(Float64(errs[2]["ConvInterp :b13"]), 14), floor); color = :black, linestyle = :dot, label = "slope 14") end Legend(fig[2, 1:2], ax1; orientation = :horizontal, nbanks = 3) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | | observed order | error at the finest grid | |:--|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl linear | 2.12 | 1.4e-06 | | BSplineKit k=4 | 3.99 | 1.1e-12 | | BSplineKit k=8 | 8.01 | 3.6e-23 | | Dierckx k=5 | 5.79 | 5.9e-16 | | ConvInterp :n3 | 3.10 | 8.5e-10 | | ConvInterp :b5 | 6.04 | 2.8e-15 | | ConvInterp :b7 | 8.11 | 3.0e-19 | | ConvInterp :b13 | 14.08 | 1.9e-30 | | fit_scattered :exact | 6.77 | 7.2e-13 | In `Float64`, `:b13` and the order-eight B-spline reach rounding on the same grid, with `:b7` two doublings behind; the 14th order shows only as a steeper approach to a floor every method reaches. In `BigFloat` the orders show in full: `:b13` on slope 14, `:b5` on slope 6, `:b7` on 8 between them, with the order-eight B-spline tracking `:b7`; the cubic methods converge at their cubic rate and the linear interpolant at its second. The order column is measured in `BigFloat`, over the last doubling that is clear of each method's floor, so the `Float64`-only methods are measured before theirs. ## Setup and query The time to construct an interpolant on jittered knots and the time to evaluate it on the two thousand fine points, in `Float64`, for 201 and for 801 knots. On a nonuniform grid the convolution kernels compute the weights of every interval at construction, in extended precision, so their setup is where the cost goes; evaluation is then the same constant-time stencil as on a uniform grid. ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The timings"} fmt(t) = t < 1e-6 ? @sprintf("%.0f ns", 1e9 * t) : t < 1e-3 ? @sprintf("%.1f μs", 1e6 * t) : t < 1 ? @sprintf("%.2f ms", 1e3 * t) : @sprintf("%.2f s", t) function timings(n) x = jittered(Float64, n); y = runge.(x) Dict(name => (itp = m(x, y); (setup = (@b $m($x, $y)).time, query = (@b $itp.($xr)).time)) for (name, m) in methods_1d) end t201 = timings(201) t801 = timings(801); ``` ::: | | setup, 201 knots | query, 201 knots | setup, 801 knots | query, 801 knots | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Interpolations.jl linear | 319 ns | 16.0 μs | 1.4 μs | 38.6 μs | | BSplineKit k=4 | 7.5 μs | 20.5 μs | 38.4 μs | 46.0 μs | | BSplineKit k=8 | 16.4 μs | 46.4 μs | 71.3 μs | 71.9 μs | | Dierckx k=5 | 32.0 μs | 189.9 μs | 106.8 μs | 351.0 μs | | ConvInterp :n3 | 1.9 μs | 27.3 μs | 2.4 μs | 54.0 μs | | ConvInterp :b5 | 90.69 ms | 73.4 μs | 448.52 ms | 95.4 μs | | ConvInterp :b7 | 207.27 ms | 94.2 μs | 790.29 ms | 110.8 μs | | ConvInterp :b13 | 724.82 ms | 200.7 μs | 2.81 s | 230.4 μs | | fit_scattered :exact | 347.3 μs | 37.5 μs | 1.22 ms | 38.2 μs | ## Time to accuracy Each method's time to construct on jittered knots and evaluate on the fine points, in `Float64`, against its largest error there, as the knots are refined. ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The work–precision study"} ns_w = ns[1:7] wp = map(ns_w) do n x = jittered(Float64, n); y = runge.(x) Dict(name => (itp = m(x, y); (err = maximum(abs.(itp.(xr) .- runge.(xr))), time = (@b $m($x, $y)).time + (@b $itp.($xr)).time)) for (name, m) in methods_1d) end fig = Figure(size = (800, 440)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "time to construct and evaluate [s]", ylabel = "largest error") for (name, _) in methods_1d scatterlines!(ax, [w[name].time for w in wp], [max(w[name].err, 1e-17) for w in wp]; markersize = 8, label = name) end Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The extended-precision construction of the nonuniform weights is the price of the kernels' order, and in `Float64` it is not worth paying for interpolation alone: the B-splines reach every accuracy down to rounding in four orders of magnitude less time, since their construction is a banded solve in the working precision, and the splines of BSplineKit.jl are the better choice for a nonuniform grid in `Float64`. Within this package, the scattered fit is the better route to the same data: its construction is a sparse solve of the size of the data, its interpolant lives on a uniform grid and evaluates on the fast path, the fastest query of any method here, and on time to accuracy it sits roughly between the two spline packages until its floor, which is set by the conditioning of the fit's collocation system rather than by the kernel. The nonuniform kernels earn their cost in two other places. Beyond `Float64`, where the order is what counts: every method needs more than a thousand knots on this function before its error passes below `Float64` rounding, and from there the gap between `:b13` and the order-eight spline widens with every doubling, as the right panel of the convergence study shows. And as the basis of `fit_scattered` on an adaptive grid, where the knots are few and chosen by the fit, and the higher order on nonuniform knots is what lets the adaptive grid beat the uniform one at equal knot count — the [scattered-data page](../../concepts/scattered.qmd) shows that comparison. The construction is paid once per grid; evaluation is the kernels' constant-time stencil, within a factor of two of the fastest method here. ## What the nonuniform kernels do not do The nonuniform path interpolates and differentiates — derivatives up to the kernel's range, as on uniform grids — but has no antiderivatives, takes the kernel's own boundary extension as its only boundary rule, and offers the `b` kernels and `:n3` only, not `:a4`, `:a5` or `:a7`. In several dimensions each axis chooses its own path, so a grid uniform along some axes and nonuniform along others costs the nonuniform construction only on the latter. The [concept page](../../concepts/nonuniform.qmd) has the details. --- *Rendered with Julia 1.13.3 on a Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-14700KF machine (28 threads), with ConvolutionInterpolations.jl 1.0.2, Interpolations.jl 0.16.3, BSplineKit.jl 0.19.3, Dierckx.jl 0.5.4, FastChebInterp.jl 1.3.1, NumericalIntegration.jl 0.3.4, HCubature.jl 1.8.0, QuadGK.jl 2.11.3, ScatteredInterpolation.jl 0.3.6, NaturalNeighbours.jl 1.3.6, Chairmarks.jl 1.3.1.*
